36832093: Summer reading 1/5. Even though I went in expecting some kind of final reveal about the murderer's identity, I still did not anticipate a reversal on this level. An enormously satisfying reading experience.
10546850: A concise and accessible introduction to astrology. Being a Capricorn sun and Leo moon feels absurdly divided; I keep swinging between "this is all feudal superstition" and "there really is something to it." I previously studied tarot out of curiosity and learned palmistry on a whim to flirt with girls. The funny thing is that, once you go far enough, different mystical systems start connecting: even Chinese lunar mansions seem to echo Western astrology. Perhaps some things really are written in the stars. At this rate I will eventually become a wandering fortune-teller.
1795079: Our Chinese teacher insisted on teaching this book right before a major exam. I did not understand a thing, but I passed in the end. So much for teaching someone to fish and then testing them on the fish.
35606579: I abandoned the ebook after two chapters. A West Coast Gary Stu meets Stanford's Chu Yuxun in "The Tyrannical Academic Overlord Falls for Me." While browsing Goodreads, I saw someone say, "I got a PhD for it," and all I could think was: girl, you made it all the way to a PhD and you still believe this?
35113983: Spring break goal 1/3. The prose has Ishiguro's usual restraint, tenderness, and quiet warmth. By April 16, procrastination had won again. After Klara arrived at Josie's home, the narrative felt rather flat, and I skimmed until slowing down for the ending. After reading Never Let Me Go, it is hard not to approach Ishiguro defensively, knowing how easily a needle can hide inside such gentle storytelling. Yet the ending was simpler than I expected. When Klara's long-foreseen future finally arrives, no greater catastrophe follows. Her worship of the Sun endures, just as the search for the meaning of human loneliness and companionship remains unresolved. If I had a Klara, she would probably watch me transform from a sunny, cheerful girl into a gloomy, sarcastic one.
36518892: I do not recommend Nietzsche to teenagers.
1394285: Maud is literally my type of guy...
1807516: I really hate people who spoil mysteries. 👊
1803641: A retrospective note: a princess's dignity is not the nobility displayed by fine clothes, but the calm and composure forged through adversity.
30303684: The first half, with its marsh setting, suspense, and paranoid outsider heroine, was perfectly tailored to my tastes. Then the romance suddenly took over, and I thought: of course romantic novels have a bigger market. Still, I finally found a huge Goodreads favorite that I could patiently finish.
10554308: I somehow forgot to rate this. Once I saw my elementary-school-aged nephew reading it with great enthusiasm and thought we might have similar tastes. Then I leaned over and discovered he was reading a sex scene. 😅
35143790: Some of its ideas feel dated, but it was written years ago and is still worth reading.
6511362: "As long as a person is alive, they remain capable of changing themselves, even radically; children are not the only ones with the capacity to grow." A brilliant critique of Freud. What resonates most with me now is the way anxiety is sustained by helplessness and resistance to change. Helplessness feels like weakness and incompetence; change means disrupting the present and conflicting with the strong, composed self I imagine I should be. The result is endless self-torment. Change hurts, but anxiety hurts more. Life is full of struggle.
1085860: A retrospective note: revenge delivered with complete satisfaction.
1427538: They became the stars and the moon.
4259314: I forgot to rate this. What kind of master of failure literature is this? To me, it reads like an endless loop of: "What should I do? I am useless, so perhaps I should die. Actually, I will finish writing the book first and die later."
27186106: The only way to take control of life is to align will and mind, directing energy toward what you truly want to do. Mental flow is the optimal experience that comes from complete concentration on work or a hobby: high ability meeting high challenge.
1927902: Respect the complexity and unknowability of human personality. People barely dare to define themselves; how can they hand that authority to a subjective questionnaire? Do not limit yourself. You can be anyone.
1258490: I finished the whole series in elementary school, reading under the covers by flashlight late into the night.
26356948: My younger sister's class assigned an essay titled "The Ferryman." I had heard this book was popular and almost bought it for her as a reference, but fortunately I read a few pages first. I understood what I was reading, yet I was still profoundly shocked.
26369699: I agree with some of its ideas, such as the claim that a superiority complex can grow from feelings of inferiority. What the authors miss is that identifying the source of an illness does not necessarily cure it; an impractical treatment can even make things worse. The idea of "chosen unhappiness" made me deeply uncomfortable. I used to be brave and forceful, and I experienced psychological trauma partly because of that. I cannot accept having that trauma described as purposeful avoidance or weakness performed to solicit sympathy. I do not lack courage. I simply refuse to let myself rest, forever forcing my naturally quiet self to swim upstream. Real courage should be rational, not a headlong charge. If every retreat is labeled fear of consequences or lack of courage, I would rather reject this reckless version of "knowing there is a tiger on the mountain and climbing it anyway." It no longer belongs within the meaning of courage.
2297697: It tells horrifying stories in the warm language of a child. To be honest, beyond the novelty and shock, I did not understand much of what it meant.
24934182: Sometimes faith does not bring the result we hope for, but it truly changes something. When you feel lost and helpless, keep walking. The direction and outcome matter less than the movement itself, because any step is forward compared with hesitating in place.
1318622: The sadness was more than my childhood self could bear.
2295163: I cannot put it into words. I love Harry Potter so, so much: the original books, fan fiction, films, games, everything. I love every vivid, living character. Even in dreams I can hear owl wings brushing past my ears. My only regret is that no letter arrived when I was eleven. For a while I truly believed the magical world was real and that Rowling must have escaped a Memory Charm by sheer luck, allowing her to create such a vast work of history.
1041007: While preparing to choose a middle school, I was so obsessed with Harry Potter that my dad hid the book on the top shelf of the wardrobe. He always used the same hiding place. Clever little me quietly pulled it out, finished it under the covers by flashlight, and put it back. To this day, Dad still thinks my successful school placement was his doing. 😂
1893466: There is something we should always keep in mind, just like... HOPE.
26349261: I happened to read the opening in elementary school, then somehow took more than a decade to finish the book. I could not let it go: wandering, suffering, hardship, luck, hope, love, fate. The warmth carried by the writing wrapped gently around my heart until I was crying with recognition. I thought about my own education, moving from a county town to overseas, living in seven or eight different places, from a three-story house to a ten-square-meter rental room. How lucky I have been to have people who love me beside me throughout it all. Time really can heal every wound. I believe everything will slowly, slowly become better.
26628823: Mother, the Sheep Man, and the bird will all leave. In the end, one must pass through the night of the new moon alone. I have been so broke lately that I can only haunt the library, but setting the story aside, charging thirty yuan when half the book is illustrations still feels a little much...
26962860: June 30: read detective fiction. July 1: if I keep obsessing over Agatha Christie, I will never finish my research reading. This cannot go on. July 2: read detective fiction.
26961102: Even the resolve to break one's chains cannot always lead to a free sky. Undying romance is ultimately no match for a carefully hidden scheme.
1015452: Murakami's prose always captures that emptiness deep inside with precision, that elusive and delicate feeling. Everyone dreams of escaping south of the border, west of the sun, yet somehow they all remain in the desert.
20421947: I stopped halfway. Unlike To Live and Chronicle of a Blood Merchant, this is not narrated in the first person. Its pace is very slow, like sitting beside a stove in winter and recalling the small details of a former life until they melt into a sigh. Each story stands alone without a fixed structure, simply narrated, yet they quietly complete one another, like a low murmur: "Did you miss that? Let me tell it again." Yu Hua remains my favorite in Chinese literature.
2046977: A retrospective note: I did not finish it. It felt a little meandering.
1076136: I read this when I was very young, and remembering it still brings a pure kind of sadness. I recall the brothers jumping from the cliff together at the end and entering the world beyond the afterlife. It may be one of the few tragic endings I encountered in children's literature, though in a way it is also open-ended: an infinite cycle.
26382433: I fought sleep and finished it in one sitting. My heart felt blocked by cotton, heavy and soft. Between the lines I caught reflections of myself: parents, control, expectations, an older brother, distorted love. Everyone has their own way of living and their own misfortune. Hope is good; without it, what could hold up the weight of a body? Hope is also the worst thing, especially when projected onto the next generation. Then it becomes the bud of disappointment and fertile ground for obsession and madness. Thankfully, my parents pulled me from the lake, and my brother dried my soaked hair.
3393056: My first idea of writing was closer to recording. Paper and pen are faithful; the question is whether one has the feeling to pick them up.
6781808: "When you go into a person's skin and walk around, then you'll really know them." Compared with racism, what I noticed in people's words and behavior from childhood was economic discrimination, so Walter was unexpectedly the character who affected me most.
1292416: To cast everything aside and love with ease, until even unconscious madness becomes a shared understanding. If genius is destined for sorrow, perhaps learning to be ordinary and worldly is something worth celebrating.
26952166: I love a short comment beneath the BBC adaptation: "Please do not touch me, suppress me, suffocate me, and pretend to love me."
25799686: My first Zijin Chen novel. The prose was, unsurprisingly, not especially impressive. In the end, the plot still relies on the power of state law as an indirect investigative tool, while Yan Liang feels like a blend of Ishigami and Yukawa. I also do not understand why Luo Wen, with such remarkable psychological resilience, would attempt suicide. After searching for his wife and daughter for so long without success, surely he must have had some sense of the truth.
3391248: Life was busy, and I was also distracted by shipping fictional couples, so I stumbled through this book over nearly two weeks. Its vivid and precise language alone makes it worth reading. I cannot say whether writing matters to me as much as the Golden Pavilion does to the narrator, but for one moment I recognized something in its reflections on beauty and art, and in the impulse to destroy what cannot be possessed. Beauty is ultimately intangible and impossible to grasp; once it comes too close and seems touchable, it can instead give birth to wrongdoing.
1083428: Perhaps this is the ancestor of the modern romance novel. I noticed its commentary on social customs and human relationships, but I am not very interested in courtship plots. Of the phrase "food, drink, men, and women," I only care about the first two words.
5363767: The quality hardly needs explaining: once again, science fiction at its peak. I do not particularly like Cheng Xin, a saintly heroine who is entrusted with enormous responsibility for no convincing reason, and the final relationship tangle among Cheng Xin, Guan Yifan, AA, and Yun Tianming feels strange. Still, these flaws do not diminish the whole.
3066477: The finest science fiction I have read so far. Every scientific concept is explained clearly and accessibly without ever becoming dry. Many details only click into place much later. No matter how explosively technology advances, what briefly saves humanity in the end is a breakthrough in cosmic theory. Such rigorous thought and formidable imagination: please call me a devoted Cixin Liu fan. P.S. Is Ye Wenjie the real final boss? 🧐
33440205: After finishing a great book in one sitting, even walking out of the bookstore feels heavier, as though the soul has left the body and traveled across mountains and rivers alone. At the same time, you feel weightless, with happiness floating like bubbles: pure, light, and spotless. I am speechless. I must write a long review. I must!
4760224: Yu Hua's prose is always so plain and unadorned, yet it strikes directly at the most fragile place in the heart. Chronicle of a Blood Merchant also exposes the absurdity of an earlier society, but it contains a great deal about human affection, especially the relationship between Xu Sanguan and Yile. I may be too sensitive; after To Live, I could not recover for a week, so I have become afraid of stories that swing between joy and sorrow. The ending is ironic, yet I was genuinely surprised that everyone remained alive and materially secure. I expected Xu Sanguan to die, which would have made it even more absurd. Yu Hua has said that the novel expresses a pursuit of equality, but I did not really see that. What I saw more clearly was criticism and genuine feeling.
4908885: I finished it in one sitting at a bookstore and left with a heavy mind. Its reputation is deserved. What stayed with me most was the absurdity of the judicial system and the constraints of blind religious morality. I feel somewhat similar to Meursault: lazy, easygoing, and indifferent to certain things. Compared with his passive, almost Zen-like life, though, I still have a little ambition. One suggestion: do not read the introduction first. Its analysis is so complete that, to preserve your own thinking, it is better saved for the end.
1084336: I read it once more while sitting in the library. After I have watched forty-four sunsets, perhaps the little fox will appear; when I look at the stars with my heart, I will find the rose that belongs to me.
10738023: I did not find it as extraordinary as people say. To me, it was the story of an obsessive man who works his way up, pursues his dream woman, and finally sacrifices himself for her. Perhaps I simply cannot understand that kind of feeling. I may reread it years from now and think differently.
1004088: I remember Pippi having an enormously long name. 😂 Such a fun book.
1085470: A very entertaining book. I love Verne's science fiction.
2159042: Saving a place for a long review. This was the first Murakami novel I finished while in the hospital.
1036274: My elementary school Chinese teacher gave this to me. The story is so compelling and the language so witty that I was completely absorbed. Like Charlotte, my teacher guided and accompanied me with love and patience. She remains the best teacher in my heart.
1141406: In some ways, this is no different from a contemporary romance novel: being short, plain, and poor does not matter, because self-respect and self-love will somehow bring a sudden inheritance and union with one's secret love. But without that inheritance, and without Rochester becoming blind, could they really have lived as equals? As a child, every assigned response focused on dignity and equality. Looking back, that feels almost ridiculous. It is nowhere near as good as Wuthering Heights.
1035848: The edition I read was illustrated, and the drawings were extremely realistic. My pure little childhood mind acquired a shadow. 😢
1008357: The prose felt rougher than in the other Chinese classics. Perhaps this kind of brotherhood, in which friends would take a blade for one another, has faded from modern life; it did not resonate deeply with me. I am probably better suited to The Story of the Stone.
3608208: Every reading offers a new way to understand the idea of a Personal Legend. I do not find the book excessively inspirational, because the story is openly fictional, allegorical, and even religious. More strictly practical readers may find that difficult to accept.
3136271: I especially liked "Rashomon" and "Hell Screen." Read against their historical background, they offer much to consider. The most baffling piece was "The Words of a Pygmy"; presented today, that format would look exactly like an inspirational quote bot. 😂
2284311: I did not understand much, and forgot much of what I read, but I did learn never to stop questioning and thinking. I should read it closely again someday.
1119839: In my memory, fairy tales were always beautiful: the prince and princess lived happily ever after. Wilde's tales alone radiate sorrowful beauty. The frozen swallow and the nightingale whose heart is pierced both die beautifully for what they desire, and the stories even carry a satirical edge. Then I understood why Wilde's work is called fairy tales for adults.
1058661: Delicate language with a faint sadness. "The Story of the Fish and the Bird" feels like the quotation bank from which generations of students have drawn love letters. Who has not used some version of "the farthest distance is not between life and death, but between you and me when you do not know I love you"? The words sound romantic, but how many people have truly considered what lies within them?
1449352: I remember our morning reading class arguing over whether Ade should be pronounced as a name or letter by letter. I miss that time.
1827374: I felt thoroughly fooled; the truth remains unreachable until the final page. That is the charm of Agatha Christie's mysteries. Poirot's decision becomes a final struggle between compassion and responsibility. Christie's detectives can soften, worry about ordinary life, and never feel impossibly remote. That is one reason I love them.
24531956: I finished the first book in sixth grade and fell straight down the rabbit hole. I wanted to hide the books in my desk and read during class. Graduation was approaching and life was busy, yet I squeezed in enough time to devour six volumes. To make me prepare for middle-school admission, Dad even hid Deathly Hallows. 😂 I should write a long review someday. P.S. On the first reading, I thought Harry should end up with Hermione. Later I understood that Harry really belonged with Ginny. Now I finally see that Harry and Draco are the true love story. Kidding. Mostly.
1046209: It has been a long time. I should open it again someday and see whether it feels different.
1060068: Reading it again. Why can I not give it one hundred stars?
1040211: A defining work of detective fiction. Sherlock Holmes remains the most iconic detective, without rival. Personally, I still prefer Agatha Christie and Keigo Higashino: alongside the puzzles, their novels depict the texture of real human life and make it easier to enter the story.
1019568: I read a young readers' edition in sixth grade and was completely captivated. For the first time, I secretly took a book to the bathroom and read by flashlight, finishing it after midnight. My mother caught me when she got up and gave me a beating. What stayed with me, beyond the physical pain, was the revelation this book gave me: the power of words.
